danish.title: Trettende bog (1812) — Kapitel 3
paragraphs: Den russiske hær blev kommanderet af Kutuzov og hans stab og desuden af kejseren fra Petersborg. Inden nyheden om Moskvas opgivelse var nået til Petersborg, var en detaljeret plan for hele felttoget blevet udarbejdet og sendt til Kutuzov som rettesnor. Skønt denne plan var udarbejdet under forudsætning af, at Moskva stadig var i vore hænder, blev den godkendt af staben og antaget som grundlag for handling. Kutuzov svarede blot, at bevægelser arrangeret på afstand altid var vanskelige at udføre. Så der blev sendt nye instrukser til løsning af de vanskeligheder, man måtte støde på, samt nye folk, der skulle overvåge Kutuzovs handlinger og aflægge beretning om dem.

Desuden blev hele den russiske hærstab nu omorganiseret. De poster, der var blevet ledige efter Bagration, der var faldet, og Barclay, der var taget af i vrede, skulle besættes. Der blev gjort meget alvorlige overvejelser om, hvorvidt det var bedre at sætte A på B's plads og B på D's, eller tværtimod at sætte D på A's plads, og så videre — som om noget mere end A's eller B's tilfredshed afhang af det.

Som følge af fjendtligheden mellem Kutuzov og Bennigsen, hans stabschef, tilstedeværelsen af kejserens fortrolige udsendinge og disse omrokeringer, var der et endnu mere indviklet partiernes spil i gang end sædvanligt i hærstaben. A underminerede B, D underminerede C, og så videre i alle tænkelige kombinationer og permutationer. I alle disse intriger var emnet som regel krigsførelsen, som alle disse mænd troede, de styrede; men denne krigens sag gik sin gang uafhængigt af dem, som den måtte: det vil sige aldrig på den måde, folk udtænkte, men altid flydende ud af massernes grundholdning. Kun i de højeste sfærer syntes alle disse planer, krydsninger og sammenfletninger at være en sand afspejling af, hvad der måtte ske.

Fyrst Mikhail Ilarionovitj! (skrev kejseren den 2. oktober i et brev, der nåede Kutuzov efter slaget ved Tarutino) Siden den 2. september har Moskva været i fjendens hænder. Dine sidste rapporter var skrevet den tyvende, og i al den tid er der hverken foretaget nogen aktion mod fjenden eller til befrielse af den ældgamle hovedstad, men ifølge dine seneste rapporter har du endda trukket dig endnu længere tilbage. Serpukhov er allerede besat af en fjendtlig afdeling, og Tula med sit berømte arsenal, der er uundværligt for hæren, er i fare. Af general Wintzingerodes rapporter ser jeg, at et fjendtligt korps på ti tusind mand rykker mod Petersborgvejen. Et andet korps på adskillige tusind mand rykker mod Dmitrov. Et tredje er rykket frem langs Vladimirvejen, og en fjerde, temmelig betydelig afdeling er opstillet mellem Ruza og Mozjajsk. Napoleon selv var i Moskva så sent som den femogtyvende. I betragtning af alle disse oplysninger, når fjenden har spredt sine styrker i store afdelinger, og med Napoleon og hans garde i Moskva — er det da muligt, at fjendens styrker over for dig er så betydelige, at de ikke tillader dig at gå til angreb? Tværtimod forfølger han sandsynligvis dig med afdelinger eller højst med et armékorps, der er langt svagere end den hær, der er betroet dig. Det forekommer, at du ved at udnytte disse omstændigheder med fordel kunne angribe en svagere fjende og tilintetgøre ham, eller i det mindste tvinge ham til tilbagetog, hvorved vi beholder en vigtig del af de provinser, der nu er besat af fjenden, og derved afværger faren fra Tula og andre byer i det indre. Du vil bære ansvaret, hvis fjenden er i stand til at rette en styrke af nogen størrelse mod Petersborg for at true denne hovedstad, hvori det ikke har været muligt at tilbageholde mange tropper; for med den hær, der er betroet dig, og når du handler med beslutsomhed og energi, har du rigelige midler til at afværge denne nye ulykke. Husk, at du stadig skal stå til regnskab over for vort krænkede fædreland for tabet af Moskva. Du har erfaret min parathed til at belønne dig. Den parathed vil ikke svækkes i mig, men jeg og Rusland har ret til at forvente af dig al den iver, fasthed og fremgang, som dit intellekt, militære talent og modigheden hos de tropper, du befaler over, berettiger os til at forvente.

Men da dette brev, der beviste, at det virkelige styrkeforhold allerede havde gjort sig gældende i Petersborg, blev afsendt, havde Kutuzov allerede fundet sig ude af stand til længere at tilbageholde den hær, han kommanderede, fra at angribe, og et slag havde fundet sted.

Den 2. oktober red en kosak, Sjapovalov, der var ude og spejde, en hare op og sårede en anden. Da han fulgte den sårede hare, trængte han langt ind i skoven og kom til den venstre flanke af Murats hær, der lå i lejr dér uden nogen forholdsregler. Kosakken fortalte leende sine kammerater, hvordan han næsten var faldet i hænderne på franskmændene. En kornet, der hørte historien, meddelte den til sin kommandør.

Kosakken blev hentet og udspurgt. Kosakofficererne ønskede at udnytte chancen til at erobre nogle heste, men en af de overordnede officerer, der kendte de højere myndigheder, rapporterede hændelsen til en general i staben. Forholdene i staben havde i den seneste tid været yderst spændte. Jermolov (general) havde besøgt Bennigsen nogle dage i forvejen og havde bønfaldt ham om at bruge sin indflydelse hos øverstkommanderende til at overtale ham til at gå i offensiven.
»Hvis jeg ikke kendte Dem, ville jeg tro, at De ikke ønskede det, De beder om. Jeg behøver blot at råde til noget, og Hans Durchlauchtighed gør det stik modsatte,« svarede Bennigsen.

Kosakkens rapport, bekræftet af hestpatruljer, der blev sendt ud, var det endelige bevis på, at begivenhederne var modne. Den stramt oprullede fjeder blev udløst, uret begyndte at snurre, og klokkerne at spille. Trods al sin formodede magt, sit intellekt, sin erfaring og sin menneskekundskab — efter at have taget kosakkens rapport i betragtning, en note fra Bennigsen, der sendte personlige rapporter til kejseren, de ønsker, han antog kejseren nærede, og det faktum, at alle generalerne udtrykte det samme ønske — kunne Kutuzov ikke længere bremse den uundgåelige bevægelse og gav ordre til at gøre det, han anså for unyttigt og skadeligt — det vil sige, han gav sin godkendelse til den allerede fuldendte kendsgerning.

english.title: Book Thirteen (1812) — Chapter 3
paragraphs: The Russian army was being commanded by Kutuzov and his staff, and also by the Emperor from Petersburg. Before news of the abandonment of Moscow had reached Petersburg, a detailed plan for the entire campaign had been drawn up and sent to Kutuzov for guidance. Though this plan assumed Moscow was still in Russian hands, it was approved by the staff and accepted as the basis for action. Kutuzov replied only that plans made at a distance were always difficult to execute. So fresh instructions were sent for handling difficulties that might arise, along with new people to watch Kutuzov's actions and report on them.

Beyond this, the entire Russian army staff was being reorganized. The positions left vacant by Bagration, who had been killed, and by Barclay, who had departed in a huff, had to be filled. Very serious thought was given to whether it would be better to put A in B's place and B in D's, or the reverse—as if anything beyond A's or B's personal satisfaction depended on these decisions.

As a result of the hostility between Kutuzov and Bennigsen (his chief of staff), the presence of the Emperor's confidential representatives, and all these personnel changes, an unusually complicated web of political maneuvering was underway among the staff. A was undermining B, D was undermining C, and so on in every possible combination. In all these intrigues, the subject was supposedly the conduct of the war, which everyone believed they were directing. But the war went on independently of them all, following its own course—never the way people planned it, but flowing always from the essential attitude of the masses. Only in the highest circles did all these schemes and machinations appear to reflect what actually had to happen.

'Prince Mikhail Ilarionovich!' wrote the Emperor on the second of October, in a letter that reached Kutuzov after the battle of Tarutino. 'Since September 2, Moscow has been in enemy hands. Your last reports were dated the twentieth, and since then no action has been taken against the enemy or to relieve the ancient capital. According to your latest dispatch, you have even retreated further. Serpukhov is already occupied by an enemy detachment, and Tula with its famous arsenal, so vital to the army, is in danger. From General Wintzingerode's reports, I see that an enemy corps of ten thousand is moving on the Petersburg road. Another of several thousand moves on Dmitrov. A third has advanced along the Vladimir road, and a fourth, quite sizable, is stationed between Ruza and Mozhaysk. Napoleon himself was in Moscow as late as the twenty-fifth. Given all this, when the enemy has scattered his forces into large detachments and Napoleon sits in Moscow with his Guards, is it really possible that the forces facing you are too strong for you to take the offensive? On the contrary, he is probably only chasing you with detachments, or at most with a corps far weaker than your army. It would seem you could advantageously attack a weaker force and destroy it, or at least force it to retreat, holding an important part of the provinces now under enemy control and averting the danger to Tula and other interior towns. You will be held responsible if the enemy manages to direct a significant force against Petersburg, where we have been unable to keep many troops. With the army entrusted to you, acting with resolution and energy, you have ample means to prevent this fresh disaster. Remember that you still must answer to our offended country for the loss of Moscow. You have seen my readiness to reward you. That readiness will not weaken, but I and Russia have a right to expect from you all the zeal, firmness, and success that your intellect, military talent, and the courage of your troops justify us in expecting.'

But by the time this letter—which showed that the real balance of forces had already made itself felt even in Petersburg—was sent, Kutuzov had found himself unable to hold back his army any longer, and a battle had already taken place.

On October second, a Cossack named Shapovalov, who was out scouting, killed one hare and wounded another. Following the wounded hare, he wandered deep into the forest and stumbled upon the left flank of Murat's army, camped there without any precautions. The Cossack laughingly told his comrades how he'd nearly fallen into French hands. A junior officer, hearing the story, passed it to his commander.

The Cossack was brought in and questioned. The Cossack officers wanted to seize the chance to capture some horses, but one of the senior officers, who had connections to the higher authorities, reported the incident to a general on the staff. Things at staff headquarters had been extremely tense lately. Ermolov had recently visited Bennigsen and begged him to use his influence to persuade the commander in chief to take the offensive.
'If I didn't know you, I'd think you didn't actually want what you're asking for. I only have to suggest something for His Highness to do the opposite,' Bennigsen replied.

The Cossack's report, confirmed by cavalry patrols sent out afterward, was the final proof that events had ripened. The tightly coiled spring was released, the clock began to whir and the chimes to play. Despite all his supposed power, his intellect, his experience, and his knowledge of men, Kutuzov—taking into account the Cossack's report, Bennigsen's note to the Emperor, the wishes he assumed the Emperor held, and the unanimous desire of all his generals—could no longer hold back the inevitable. He gave the order to do what he considered useless and harmful—he approved, that is, the accomplished fact.
